name: Artaxerxes (Persian king)
title: Persian Great King and Restorer of Jerusalem
summary: Artaxerxes I Longimanus was a Persian great king of the Achaemenid dynasty who had decisive influence on the restoration of the Jewish people after the Babylonian exile. At the beginning of his reign, he temporarily halted the rebuilding of Jerusalem following accusations from local opponents that the city had a history of rebellion. Later, he changed course and issued a comprehensive decree granting the priest and scribe Ezra full authority and abundant resources to lead a group of Jews back to Jerusalem to strengthen temple service and instruction in God's law. He also sent his trusted cupbearer Nehemiah as governor to Judah with authority and building materials to rebuild Jerusalem's walls. Artaxerxes' shifting, yet ultimately supportive attitude toward the Jewish people appears in the biblical text as an instrument in God's plan to restore His people in the promised land.

keyEvents.title: Temporarily halted the rebuilding of Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: In the early part of his reign, Artaxerxes received a letter from opponents of the Jews warning that Jerusalem had historically been a rebellious city. He ordered that the work to rebuild the city and its walls be stopped until further notice.

keyEvents.title: Granted Ezra authority to travel to Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Artaxerxes issued a decree allowing the priest and scribe Ezra to lead a group of Jews back to Jerusalem, providing generous gifts for the temple and full authority to appoint judges and teach the people God's law.

keyEvents.title: Funded temple service
keyEvents.description: The king ordered that Ezra should receive silver, gold, wheat, wine, oil, and salt from the royal treasuries west of the Euphrates to ensure proper worship at the temple in Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Sent Nehemiah to Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: When Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, expressed grief over Jerusalem's ruined condition and asked for permission to go there to rebuild its walls, Artaxerxes not only granted him leave but also gave him letters to the governors and timber from the king's forests for construction.

keyEvents.title: Appointed Nehemiah as governor of Judah
keyEvents.description: Artaxerxes gave Nehemiah the position of governor in the province of Judah, a role he held for twelve years—from the 20th to the 32nd year of the king's reign—under the king's protection and support.

versions.summary: Artaxerxes I was a Persian king who played a crucial role in the rebuilding of Jerusalem. He authorized Ezra to travel to Jerusalem with a group of Jews, and later sent Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem's walls. His goodwill toward the Jewish people was an important part of God's plan for Israel's restoration after the exile.
versions.title: The Benevolent Ruler of Persia
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Benevolent Ruler of Persia' is somewhat informal and one-sidedly positive. Artaxerxes also temporarily halted the rebuilding, so 'benevolent' gives an incomplete picture. A more neutral title might be better.; [major] Artaxerxes was not just a general 'king', but specifically a Persian Great King (Great King of Persia). He was also an important protector/benefactor for the Jewish people. The roles should be expanded.; [major] Ezra 4:7-23 concerns the halt in rebuilding the city and its walls, not the temple construction. The temple had already been completed under Darius I (Ezra 6:15). The description should be clarified to specify that it concerned the rebuilding of the city, not the temple building.; [minor] The father is correctly given as Xerxes (Ahasuerus). This is historically accurate. According to historical sources, the mother was Amestris, but she is not mentioned in the Bible, so zero is acceptable.; [minor] The summary is good, but could be improved by noting that Artaxerxes also temporarily halted the rebuilding work before later allowing it, which gives a more nuanced picture.; [major] The description says 'rebuilding work' generally, but the title says 'temple construction'. Ezra 4:7-23 specifically concerns the rebuilding of the city and its walls, not the temple. The title must be corrected.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are important historical, archaeological, and linguistic details about Artaxerxes I that should be included.

versions.summary: Artaxerxes I was a Persian great king of the Achaemenid dynasty who played an important role in Israel's restoration after the exile. Early in his reign, he temporarily halted the rebuilding of Jerusalem following complaints from local opponents. Later, he gave the priest Ezra authority and resources to travel to Jerusalem with a group of Jews to strengthen worship and the teaching of the law. He also sent his cupbearer Nehemiah to Jerusalem as governor with authority and materials to rebuild the city's walls. His changing, but ultimately favorable attitude toward the Jewish people is seen as an important link in God's plan for Israel's restoration.

versions.reason: [minor] The expression 'as governorship' is grammatically incorrect. It should be 'as governor'. 'Governorship' is a noun describing the office/position, not the person.; [minor] 'Appointed Nehemiah to governorship in Judah' should be 'Appointed Nehemiah as governor in Judah'. 'Governorship' refers to the office, not the person holding it.; [minor] The description uses 'the position of governorship', which should be 'the position of governor'. Same grammatical error as in the title and summary.; [minor] The role 'political protector of Jerusalem's rebuilding' could be supplemented with a role reflecting his authority over the province of Judah, for example, 'ruler under the Achaemenid Empire' to emphasize the imperial perspective.; [minor] Historical sources mention Amestris as the mother of Artaxerxes I. Although she is not a biblical figure, this could have been noted with a footnote. The current note is acceptable but may warrant comment.; [minor] The final footnote regarding the Esther connection is interesting but somewhat speculative. The phrasing 'stepson or descendant' is imprecise – if Esther was queen married to Xerxes I, Artaxerxes would potentially have been Esther's stepson, not her biological son. The wording could be clarified.

footnotes.text: Artaxerxes I (c. 465–424 BC), also known as Artaxerxes Longimanus ('Long-handed'), ruled over the Achaemenid Persian Empire for more than 40 years. According to Greek historians, his nickname refers to his right hand being longer than his left.

The decree that Artaxerxes gave to Ezra (Ezra 7:12–26) is presented in Aramaic in the biblical text, reflecting that Aramaic was the official administrative language of the Persian Empire. This is one of the Aramaic passages in the book of Ezra.

Artaxerxes I is identified with the Persian king Ardashir in Persian inscriptions. Archaeological findings from Persepolis and other sites confirm his reign and administrative practice of issuing decrees to subject peoples.

In Jewish tradition, Artaxerxes' goodwill is seen as an expression of God's providence. Nehemiah's appointment as governor in the 20th year of Artaxerxes' reign (445 BC) holds special significance in chronological calculations related to Daniel's prophecy of the seventy weeks (Dan 9:25).

Some scholars have debated whether Artaxerxes in Ezra 4:7 might refer to a different Persian king than Artaxerxes I, but the prevailing view is that it refers to Artaxerxes I Longimanus, who reigned from 465–424 BC.

The father of Artaxerxes I was Xerxes I (Hebrew: Ahasuerus), whom many biblical scholars identify with the king in the book of Esther. If this identification is correct, Artaxerxes would have been the stepson of Queen Esther, creating a remarkable connection between the book of Esther and the story of restoration.

The role of cupbearer that Nehemiah held at Artaxerxes' court was a highly trusted position in the Persian royal system. The cupbearer tasted the king's wine to rule out poisoning and thus had personal access to the ruler—explaining why Nehemiah could present his case directly to the king.
